text: The single most famous experiment in quantum mechanics uses nothing more exotic than a wall with two slits in it — and it proves particles are not simply tiny bullets following definite paths.

Fire electrons one at a time at a wall with two narrow slits, with a detector screen behind it. Classical bullets would give two bright bands lined up with the slits. Instead, over many thousands of particles, you get an interference pattern — alternating bands of high and low density, like two overlapping water ripples. This happens even when particles go through one at a time, with long gaps between them, so nothing is bumping into anything else. Each individual particle still lands as a single dot — but the overall pattern is wave-like.

Now add a detector at the slits that records which slit each particle actually used. The interference pattern vanishes completely, replaced by the plain two-band pattern. This isn't the detector physically disturbing the particles — it holds however gently the information is extracted. The mere fact that a definite which-path answer exists, anywhere, is what destroys the interference. Turn that detector back off, and the interference pattern returns, with nothing about the trajectories having changed.

A few years earlier, Louis de Broglie proposed that matter itself has a wave character: every particle with momentum has an associated wavelength, inversely related to that momentum. Electron beams fired at crystals confirmed it directly, producing diffraction patterns with exactly the spacing de Broglie predicted. Every piece of matter has this wave character in principle — it's just unobservably small for anything larger than a molecule.

So what does wave-particle duality actually mean? A quantum object is described by a complex-valued amplitude spread across every path available to it — in the double-slit case, a nonzero amplitude passing through both slits at once. These amplitudes combine like waves, adding or canceling, which is exactly the interference on the screen. The particle side only shows up at measurement: one definite, localized outcome, never a smeared half-detection. This isn't a historical footnote — it's the literal operating principle of every quantum algorithm: wrong answers interfere destructively, the right answer interferes constructively, and then you measure.
Next lesson turns this into precise rules: the five postulates that define what quantum mechanics actually is as a mathematical theory.
